c.tagline: Dutch Caribbean capital and gateway to world-class shore diving.

taxi.fareNote: Bonaire has no Uber or ride-hailing; taxis (license plates begin with 'TX') are unmetered with government-set fixed fares by zone — confirm the price before you set off. Most visitors rent a car or pickup, the standard way to reach the dive sites and national park. The US dollar is the local currency and English is widely spoken.

emergency.note: 911 reaches police and fire, and 912 is the ambulance line; English is widely spoken and the US dollar is the official currency.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Never leave valuables in parked rental pickups at dive sites — vehicle break-ins are the main petty crime.

hood_desc: The compact, colorful capital and cruise port strung along the seafront, with Fort Oranje, Wilhelmina Square, waterfront restaurants, dive shops and most of the island's shops and bars; best for first-timers who want to be walkable to dining and the dive boats.

A tranquil residential and vacation-rental district just south of town along the coast near Flamingo Airport, lined with small oceanfront resorts and easy shore-diving entries; suits families and divers wanting a quiet seaside base.

The seaside neighborhood immediately north of downtown, home to several of the island's dive resorts and some of its most famous house reefs; good for divers who want to roll off the dock and stay near the center.
Bonaire's largest residential district, an inland local neighborhood away from the waterfront with everyday shops and a slower, authentic pace; suits budget travelers and longer stays.
An upscale, low-density residential area on the coast north of Kralendijk with villas, calm bays and Santa Barbara-style quiet; suits those after a private, scenic retreat with a rental car.
lodging: Courtyard by Marriott Bonaire Dive Resort

water.note: Tap water is distilled seawater and among the Caribbean's best.

transit.pay: There is no formal fixed-route city bus network; a limited public/shared minibus service runs irregularly, paid in cash (US dollars) to the driver. Almost every visitor rents a car or pickup, or uses taxis. There is no rechargeable transit card.
transit.hours: Any shared minibus service is sporadic and daytime-only; taxis and rental cars fill every other gap, including nights.
transit.note: Bonaire has no metro, tram, rail or reliable scheduled city bus; getting around means renting a car or pickup (the island norm, needed to reach dive sites and the national park), taxis with fixed zone fares, or bicycles and scooters in and around Kralendijk.

car.idp: Not required (US, Canadian, EU and most licenses valid up to 6 months)

ferry: Water taxi to Klein Bonaire (seasonal, from the downtown waterfront)

transit.m: Taxi to Kralendijk / downtown (~5-10 min, fixed fare)
Taxi to Belnem or Hato resorts (~10 min, fixed fare)

tip.r: A 10-15% service charge is often added to restaurant bills; if not, 10-15% is standard, and rounding up for taxis, dive crews and housekeeping is appreciated.

landmarks: Bonaire National Marine Park
Ringing the entire island, this pioneering protected reef offers more than 80 shore-accessible dive sites, crowning Bonaire the world's shore-diving capital.
Klein Bonaire and No Name Beach
A water taxi skims to this uninhabited islet's dazzling white beach, where pristine coral gardens begin just steps from shore.
Fort Oranje
Kralendijk's little 17th-century Dutch fort, guarded by cannons and a stone lighthouse, anchors the colourful ochre-and-white waterfront of the capital.
Salt Pans and Slave Huts
Blinding white salt pyramids rise beside tiny 1850s stone huts that housed enslaved salt workers, a stark and moving southern-coast landmark.
Pekelmeer Flamingo Sanctuary
One of the Caribbean's few flamingo breeding grounds paints the southern salt lagoons pink with thousands of elegant wading birds.
Lac Bay (Sorobon Beach)
A shallow turquoise lagoon fringed by mangroves serves up world-class windsurfing conditions and laid-back beach shacks on Bonaire's east coast.
1000 Steps Beach
Only 67 limestone steps actually descend to this storied cove, where snorkellers and divers meet turtles over brilliant coral terraces.
Seru Largu Viewpoint
Bonaire's beloved hilltop lookout, crowned by a millennium monument, surveys Kralendijk, Klein Bonaire and the turquoise leeward coast.
Terramar Museum
On the waterfront boulevard, this crisp modern museum spins 7,000 years of Caribbean and Bonairean history from Amerindians to colonial times.
Kaya Grandi
Kralendijk's main street, lined with pastel Dutch colonial buildings, boutiques, and cafes, its walls covered in large murals of the island's flamingos.

train.note: Bonaire has no railway. Arrive by air into Flamingo International Airport, with flights from Amsterdam, Curaçao and the United States, or by cruise ship. There is no rail anywhere in the Dutch Caribbean.

bus.note: No international coaches, and Bonaire has only a minimal public bus service on the island - most visitors hire a car or pickup, which is effectively expected here given how spread out the dive sites are. Taxis operate on fixed government rates. There is no terminal.

intl.op: water-taxi operators — tickets at the pier

ferry.note: There is no scheduled international ferry - the ABC islands are linked by air, and the Curaçao passenger service has not run reliably. The Klein Bonaire water taxi is a short hop to the uninhabited island opposite Kralendijk, which is a marine park and has no facilities, so take water with you. Dive boats operate as charters.

full.name: Washington Slagbaai National Park
full.blurb: A rugged wilderness park across the island's north, with flamingo salinas, cactus hills, remote dive and snorkel bays and Bonaire's highest point, Brandaris.

full.name: Southern Salt Flats & Flamingo Sanctuary
full.blurb: Blindingly white salt pans, pink flamingos, historic slave huts and turquoise shore-dive sites strung along the island's southern loop road.
